question: Maintaining the competitiveness of Spanish and EU ports in relation to thirdcountry ports

In recent years, third-country ports in the Mediterranean and North Africa have received European funding. In 2023, the container terminal in the Egyptian port of Damietta obtained a loan of EUR 125 million from the EBRD, an institution in which the EU is a shareholder.

In Morocco, the Nador West Med mega-port received loans from the EBRD of EUR 310 million in 2015, 2022 and 2025, in addition to a grant of EUR 5 million. The Tanger Med port complex also received EIB support, receiving EUR 40 million in 2007 and EUR 200 million in 2010.

This support stands in contrast to the strict obligations EU ports face under the maritime ETS and FuelEU Maritime initiatives, creating an uneven playing field in relation to facilities in North Africa that are not subject to these requirements. The Spanish ports potentially affected by this include Algeciras, Valencia, Barcelona, Cádiz, Huelva, Malaga, Las Palmas and Santa Cruz de Tenerife. In view of the above: 1.
What is the Commission’s view on the fact that European resources are being allocated to third-country ports that are in competition with EU ports?
What measures will the Commission take to strengthen the competitiveness of Spanish and EU ports and prevent losses in competitiveness in relation to third-country facilities?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.6.2026) The Commission recognises the importance of EU ports as hubs for global trade. When EU resources support third-country ports, this is creating new opportunities and markets, ensuring their development is aligned with EU interests, rather than leaving these opportunities to other players like China, the Middle East or the United States.

Economic development in North Africa contributes to job creation and regional stability, indirectly supporting EU economic security. Investments are embedded in a broader strategy aimed at sustainable growth, climate resilience and convergence with EU standards. This can open investment opportunities for EU firms supporting EU jobs and indirectly supporting EU economic security.

The Commission closely monitors these investments to ensure coherence with EU industrial policy and competitiveness of EU ports. In this context, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the European Investment Bank (EIB) invest resources in line with their mandates, which include furthering global investment and cooperation and supporting developing countries.

EU companies can apply for such funding, and many port authorities have received EIB loans, including in Spain (e.g. Malaga in 2024). The EU Ports Strategy1 has a strong focus on strengthening the competitiveness of EU ports and addresses the need to consider the impact on their competitiveness when deciding on the allocation of resources from EU or Member States budgets to third countries.

The risk of evasion from Emissions Trading System (ETS) or Fuel EU rules is being monitored by the Commission2. The upcoming ETS review will also assess what other measures may be taken in this regard3. 1 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and

Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions - EU Ports Strategy, COM/2026/112 final, available at: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52026DC0112. 2 The first report on the implementation of ETS in maritime transport of March 2025 covered the potential risk of evasion, including diversion of transhipment activity from EU to neighbouring non-EU ports.

It did not identify evasive behaviour attributable to the implementation of EU rules. The Commission welcomes similar efforts by Member States, in particular Spain’s ETS observatory, set up by Puertos del Estado.

3 The ETS Directive (Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 October 2003 establishing a scheme for greenhouse gas emission allowance trading within the Community and amending Council Directive 96/61/EC, as amended, consolidate version available at: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?

uri=CELEX%3A02003L0087-20240301 ) and FuelEU Maritime Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 September 2023 on the use of renewable and low-carbon fuels in maritime transport, and amending Directive 2009/16/EC, available at https://eurlex.europa.

eu/eli/reg/2023/1805/oj/eng ) address the potential risk of evasion in transhipment activity, by providing for the identification of neighbouring ports where stops by containerships are not counted as the start or end of an in-scope voyage. Tanger Med (Morocco) and East Port Said (Egypt) have been designated as such ports. The list will be updated regularly.

EU State aid rules allow Member States to support ports under the General Block Exemption Regulation (GBER)4, provided the applicable conditions are met. Projects non eligible under GBER can be notified to the Commission for State aid assessment.
